function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

I’m sorry, but I don’t have the ability to clone repositories, inspect their contents, or make commits to a remote GitHub repository from here. ---

## 1️⃣ Clone the Repository

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> **Tip:** If you’re using HTTPS instead of SSH, replace the URL accordingly.

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse & Create Files

Below is a minimal setup that should work for a typical “welcome” Node.js app (likely an Express server).  
Feel free to adjust paths, ports, or image tags to match your exact project structure.

### 2.1 Dockerfile

Create a file named `Dockerfile` at the root of the repo:

```dockerfile
# Use official lightweight Node runtime
FROM node:18-alpine

# Set working directory inside the container
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Copy package metadata first so we can cache npm install
COPY package*.json ./

# Install dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy source code
COPY . .

# Expose the port your app listens on (adjust if needed)
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the application
CMD ["npm", "start"]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> * `node:18-alpine` is small and fast.  
> * `npm ci` ensures reproducible installs.  
> * `--only=production` skips devDependencies unless you need them.  
> * Adjust the `EXPOSE` and `CMD` lines if your app uses a different start script or port.

### 2.2 Kubernetes YAML

Create a file named `k8s-nodejs-welcome.yaml` (or split into separate `deployment.yaml` and `service.yaml`):

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: <YOUR_REGISTRY>/nodejs-welcome:latest   # Replace with your image registry/tag
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer          # Change to NodePort/ClusterIP as needed
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80                  # External port
    targetPort: 3000          # Container port
```

> **What to change?**  
> * Replace `<YOUR_REGISTRY>/nodejs-welcome:latest` with the actual image you’ll push to Docker Hub, ECR, GCR, etc.  
> * If you want a NodePort instead of LoadBalancer, set `type: NodePort` and optionally specify `nodePort`.

### 2.3 GitHub Actions Workflow

Create `.github/workflows/docker-build.yml`:

```yaml
name: Build & Push Docker Image

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
    - name: Checkout code
      uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Set up Docker Buildx
      uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

    - name: Log in to Docker Hub
      uses: docker/login-action@v3
      with:
        username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}
        password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}

    - name: Cache Docker layers
      uses: actions/cache@v3
      with:
        path: /tmp/.buildx-cache
        key: ${{ runner.os }}-buildx-${{ github.sha }}
        restore-keys: |
          ${{ runner.os }}-buildx-

    - name: Build and push Docker image
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
      with:
        context: .
        push: true
        tags: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}/nodejs-welcome:latest
```

> **Prerequisites**  
> * Add two repository secrets: `DOCKERHUB_USERNAME` and `DOCKERHUB_TOKEN`.  
> * Ensure your Dockerfile is at the repo root (as above).  

---

## 3️⃣ Commit & Push Changes

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s-nodejs-welcome.yaml .github/workflows/docker-build.yml
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

If you prefer to keep the Kubernetes YAML in a dedicated folder, adjust the paths accordingly.

---

## 4️⃣ Verify

* After pushing, check the Actions tab on GitHub – you should see the workflow run successfully.  
* Once the image is built and pushed, you can deploy it to your cluster:

```bash
kubectl apply -f k8s-nodejs-welcome.yaml
```

---
